working_question: How does social media affect mental health among college students, with attention to anxiety, depression, sleep, and social comparison?

context.assignment: Psychology 190 capstone prep; 8-10 scholarly, preferably peer-reviewed sources in APA style
context.breadth_basis: Focused landscape by default; comprehensive selected deep work simulated with the assignment's narrowed-topic context.
context.interaction_basis: The test simulates intake and narrowed-topic context from assignment-prompts.md rather than an actual live multi-turn conversation.

breadth_tier: focused landscape; comprehensive selected deep work

queries.text: ((((("social media") OR ("social networking sites"))) AND ((("mental health") OR (anxiety) OR (depression)))) AND ((("college students") OR ("undergraduate students"))))
queries.decision: Selected 7 records and ran two component searches because the first page retained relevant but conceptually separable branches.

queries.decision: Selected 5 records; the page produced direct student evidence and multiple review/meta-analytic candidates.

sources.citation: Ridout, B., & Campbell, A. (2018). The use of social networking sites in mental health interventions for young people: Systematic review. *Journal of Medical Internet Research, 20*(12), e12244. https://doi.org/10.2196/12244
sources.title: The Use of Social Networking Sites in Mental Health Interventions for Young People: Systematic Review
sources.evidence_base: 9 articles describing 5 SNS-based interventions for people up to age 25; quantitative meta-analysis was not possible.
sources.credibility: Peer-reviewed venue; explicit systematic-review methods and acknowledged evidence limitations.
sources.selection_reason: Systematic review of SNS-based youth mental-health interventions; directly maps an intervention branch.

sources.citation: Weinstein, A. M. (2023). Problematic social networking site use-effects on mental health and the brain. *Frontiers in Psychiatry, 13*, Article 1106004. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyt.2022.1106004
sources.title: Problematic Social Networking Site use-effects on mental health and the brain
sources.evidence_base: Narrative review of evidence on problematic SNS use; includes limited brain-imaging evidence and preliminary CBT evidence.
sources.credibility: Peer-reviewed venue; review is described as broad but not systematic in the abstract.
sources.selection_reason: Review linking problematic SNS use to depression, anxiety, stress, sleep, and emerging brain-function evidence.

sources.citation: Kim, T., & Hong, H. (2021). Understanding university students' experiences, perceptions, and attitudes toward peers displaying mental health-related problems on social networking sites: Online survey and interview study. *JMIR Mental Health, 8*(10), e23465. https://doi.org/10.2196/23465
sources.title: Understanding University Students’ Experiences, Perceptions, and Attitudes Toward Peers Displaying Mental Health–Related Problems on Social Networking Sites: Online Survey and Interview Study
sources.evidence_base: 226 survey respondents and 20 interview participants at six universities in South Korea.
sources.credibility: Peer-reviewed venue; includes survey and interview methods.
sources.selection_reason: Survey and interview study of peer recognition, stigma, and support on SNSs; represents a social-context branch.

sources.citation: Ojha, K., Soohinda, G., Sampath, H., & Dutta, S. (2021). Social networking sites and its relation to social comparison and psychological well-being among medical university students. *Indian Journal of Psychiatry, 63*(6), 593-596. https://doi.org/10.4103/indianjpsychiatry.indianjpsychiatry_1344_20
sources.title: Social networking sites and its relation to social comparison and psychological well-being among medical university students
sources.evidence_base: 220 medical students in India; mean age 20.44 years.
sources.credibility: Peer-reviewed venue; cross-sectional design limits causal inference.
sources.selection_reason: Cross-sectional student study linking SNS use, impression management, social comparison, depression, and anxiety.

sources.citation: Zhou, M., Li, F., Wang, Y., Chen, S., & Wang, K. (2020). Compensatory social networking site use, family support, and depression among college freshman: Three-wave panel study. *Journal of Medical Internet Research, 22*(9), e18458. https://doi.org/10.2196/18458

sources.credibility: Peer-reviewed venue; longitudinal panel design strengthens temporal inference.
sources.selection_reason: Three-wave college-freshman panel study testing compensatory SNS use, family support, and depression.

sources.citation: Hunt, M. G., Marx, R., Lipson, C., & Young, J. (2018). No more FOMO: Limiting social media decreases loneliness and depression. *Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, 37*(10), 751-768. https://doi.org/10.1521/jscp.2018.37.10.751
sources.title: No More FOMO: Limiting Social Media Decreases Loneliness and Depression
sources.container: Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology
sources.evidence_base: 143 undergraduates at the University of Pennsylvania randomized to limited use or usual use for three weeks.
sources.credibility: Peer-reviewed venue; randomized experimental design, but abstract-level access limits full-method review.

sources.container: European Journal of Investigation in Health, Psychology and Education

sources.container: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health

sources.evidence_base: Studies 1-3 included 347, 180, and 233 Chinese college/university students respectively.

themes.name: Problematic use and mental health
themes.description: Retrieved sources discuss associations between excessive or problematic SNS use and mental-health symptoms.

themes.name: Social comparison, envy, and self-esteem
themes.description: Retrieved sources link comparison and envy on SNSs to self-esteem, depression, and anxiety.

themes.name: Sleep quality and timing
themes.description: Retrieved sources connect social-media timing, fatigue, problematic use, and sleep quality among students.

themes.name: Interventions and limiting use
themes.description: Retrieved sources evaluate limiting use or using SNS platforms to deliver mental-health support.

themes.name: Social support and compensatory use
themes.description: Retrieved sources discuss family support, peer support, and SNS use as compensation during college transition.

themes.name: Peer disclosure and stigma
themes.description: One retrieved source examines how students recognize and respond to peers' mental-health disclosures on SNSs.

questions.text: Does limiting social media use improve well-being?
How do social comparison and self-esteem relate to depression and anxiety?
How is social media use related to sleep quality and timing?
How does fear of missing out connect social media use with mental-health outcomes?
How do social support and compensatory use relate to depression during college transition?
How do students recognize and respond to peers' mental-health disclosures on SNSs?

selected_paths.scope: Comparison, self-esteem, FOMO, and sleep pathways, with intervention and social-context sources for breadth.

selection_decisions.reason: Systematic review of SNS-based youth mental-health interventions; directly maps an intervention branch.
Review linking problematic SNS use to depression, anxiety, stress, sleep, and emerging brain-function evidence.
Survey and interview study of peer recognition, stigma, and support on SNSs; represents a social-context branch.
Cross-sectional student study linking SNS use, impression management, social comparison, depression, and anxiety.
Three-wave college-freshman panel study testing compensatory SNS use, family support, and depression.
Randomized experiment testing whether limiting social media improves loneliness, depression, anxiety, and FOMO.
Systematic review of envy, social comparison, and depression, including evidence on direction and moderators.
Three-college-student study set testing self-esteem and FOMO as mediators between SNS use and depression.
Systematic review organizing SNS-use effects on self-esteem through comparison, feedback, and self-reflection.
Meta-analysis testing whether SNS-use indicators predict well-being after accounting for social support and self-esteem.
Foundational undergraduate study of social-media timing and sleep quality; retained as a 2016 exception to the preferred date range.
Cross-sectional study linking problematic SNS use with sleep quality and mental-health symptoms.

limitations: No keyed Primo Search API was available; the keyless PNX REST fallback was used.
All annotations are abstract-level; no full text was reviewed.
The 2016 sleep source is a deliberate exception to the preferred 2018-2026 range because it directly studies undergraduate sleep timing.
The Primo PNX response includes primarily local and Primo Central metadata; result counts should not be treated as complete field coverage.
The landscape is not exhaustive and is best understood as purpose-aware saturation for the undergraduate assignment.
The test simulated intake and narrowed-topic context from assignment-prompts.md rather than a live multi-turn conversation.
